meta.titre: Gravitational Fields: Field Strength, Potential, Orbits and Escape Speed
meta.sous_theme: Gravitational fields: field, potential and orbits

sections.contenu_markdown: When the Cameroon Radio Television broadcasts a football match of the Indomitable Lions by satellite, the signal goes up to a satellite that seems to hang motionless above the equator, about $36\,000\ \mathrm{km}$ above the ground, and your dish at Yaounde or Garoua points at that fixed spot all year. Why can a satellite stay up there, and why do astronauts float inside a station that is still held by Earth's gravity? The same inverse-square law explains the fall of an apple, the orbit of the Moon and the choice of that height. In the GCE examination this theme brings together the definition of field strength, graphs of field and potential, and circular orbits.

items: A body moving in a circle of radius $r$ at speed $v$ has a centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ directed towards the centre, and the force producing it is $mv^2/r$.
The period $T$ of a circular motion is the time for one revolution, and the speed is $v=2\pi r/T$.
Kinetic energy is $\frac12 mv^2$ and the work done by a force is force times displacement in the direction of the force.

sections.titre: Newton's law, field strength, potential and circular orbits
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Newton's law of gravitation.** Two point masses $M$ and $m$ a distance $r$ apart attract each other with a force
$$F=\frac{GMm}{r^2},\qquad G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}$$
The law applies to uniform spheres with $r$ measured between their centres.

**Gravitational field strength** $g$ at a point is the force per unit mass on a small test mass placed there, $g=F/m$, in $\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ (the same as $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$). It always points towards the attracting mass. Outside a spherical body of mass $M$ and radius $R$ (for $r\ge R$) it is
$$g=\frac{GM}{r^2}$$
as if all the mass were at the centre. For Earth, $M=5.97\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $R=6.37\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ give $g=9.81\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ at the surface. Inside a sphere of uniform density, $g$ is proportional to the distance from the centre. So a graph of $g$ against $r$ for a uniform spherical planet (a good first model of the Earth) rises along a straight line from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface and then falls as $1/r^2$.

**Gravitational potential** $\phi$ at a point is the work done per unit mass by an external agent in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. Because gravity is attractive, $\phi$ is negative:
$$\phi=-\frac{GM}{r}$$
The field is the negative gradient of the potential, $g=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}r}$, and the change of potential energy when a mass $m$ moves between two points is $m\,\Delta\phi$.

**Circular orbits.** The gravitational force on the satellite provides the centripetal force:
$$\frac{GMm}{r^2}=\frac{mv^2}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}\ \Rightarrow\ T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\,r^3$$
so $T^2\propto r^3$ (Kepler's third law). Note that the acceleration of the satellite is $v^2/r$, directed to the centre; its speed is constant but its velocity changes direction.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why astronauts seem weightless, or for the height and the conditions of a communications satellite orbit.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
An astronaut in orbit still has a gravitational pull on her (about $8.20\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ at a height of $600\ \mathrm{km}$). She seems weightless because she and the spacecraft are in free fall together with the same acceleration towards the Earth, so the floor exerts no contact force on her. Her apparent weight, the reaction force from the floor, is zero.

A **geostationary** satellite (i) orbits above the equator, (ii) moves from west to east in the same sense as the Earth's rotation, and (iii) has a period of $24\ \mathrm{h}$ (strictly the sidereal day, $23\ \mathrm{h}\ 56\ \mathrm{min}$), so it stays above the same point on the Earth. With $T=24\ \mathrm{h}=86\,400\ \mathrm{s}$, the relation $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/GM$ gives
$$r=\left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}=4.22\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$$
a height of $3.6\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$ above the surface, and its orbital speed is $3070\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks for the energy needed to lift a mass out of the field or for the minimum launch speed.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
To move a mass $m$ from the surface (potential $-GM/R$) to infinity (potential $0$) the work needed is $m\,\Delta\phi=GMm/R$. The escape speed is the launch speed for which the initial kinetic energy equals this work, ignoring air resistance:
$$\tfrac12mv_e^2=\frac{GMm}{R}\ \Rightarrow\ v_e=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}$$
For the Earth, $\phi=-6.25\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at the surface and $v_e=1.12\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The escape speed does not depend on the mass of the body that escapes.

sections.enonce_markdown: A satellite is in a circular orbit 600 km above the Earth's surface. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}$, $M_E=5.97\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$. (a) Find the gravitational field strength at the satellite. (b) Find its orbital speed. (c) Find its period in minutes.

etapes.justification: Distances in the law are measured from the centre of the Earth, not from the surface.

etapes.action: Calculate the field strength for part (a).
etapes.justification: Outside the Earth the field is that of a point mass at the centre, $g=GM/r^2$.

etapes.action: Equate gravity to the centripetal force for part (b).
etapes.justification: Gravity is the only force on the satellite, and the acceleration of the circular motion is $v^2/r$, which equals the field strength $g$.
In one period the satellite travels the circumference $2\pi r$ at constant speed.
The relation $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/GM$ must give the same period.

sections.conclusion_markdown: At this height the field strength is **8.20 N kg$^{-1}$** (less than the surface value), the orbital speed is **7560 m s$^{-1}$** and the period is **96.6 minutes**.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the height above the surface as $r$ in $GM/r^2$ (for example $r=600\ \mathrm{km}$).
items.pourquoi_faux: In Newton's law $r$ is the distance between centres of mass. The Earth's radius must be added to the height.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that astronauts float because there is no gravity in space.
items.pourquoi_faux: At the height of a space station gravity is still more than $80\%$ of its value at the surface; it is the force that keeps the station in orbit.
items.correction_markdown: The astronaut and the spacecraft are in free fall with the same acceleration, so there is no contact force and the apparent weight is zero.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing the acceleration of a satellite as $v/R^2$ or saying that it is zero because its speed is constant.
items.pourquoi_faux: The acceleration of circular motion is $v^2/r$ towards the centre. The speed is constant but the direction of the velocity changes, so the velocity changes and there is an acceleration.
items.correction_markdown: Use $a=v^2/r=g$ for a satellite, directed to the centre, and $F=mv^2/r$ for the centripetal force.

items.erreur_markdown: Drawing the field strength inside the Earth as inverse-square (falling) all the way to the centre.
items.pourquoi_faux: The $1/r^2$ law applies outside a spherical mass. Inside a sphere of uniform density only the mass nearer the centre than the point counts, so $g$ becomes smaller as you go in.
items.correction_markdown: Inside: $g$ increases linearly with $r$ from zero at the centre. At the surface: maximum. Outside: $g\propto1/r^2$.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving a positive value for the gravitational potential at a point near a planet.
items.pourquoi_faux: The zero of potential is at infinity and gravity is attractive, so work must be supplied to remove a mass; potentials near a mass are below zero.
items.correction_markdown: $\phi=-GM/r$, a negative number such as $-6.25\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at the Earth's surface.

items.enonce_markdown: The gravitational field strength at the surface of the Earth is $9.8\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. Calculate (a) the field strength at a point which is a distance equal to the Earth's radius above the surface and (b) the gravitational force on a $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ astronaut at that point.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The distance from the centre is $r=2R_E$, twice its distance when on the surface. Since $g\propto1/r^2$,
$$g=9.8\times\left(\frac{R_E}{2R_E}\right)^2=\frac{9.8}{4}=\mathbf{2.45\ N\,kg^{-1}}$$

(b) $F=mg=70\times2.45=\mathbf{172\ N}$.

items.enonce_markdown: The Moon has mass $7.35\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $1.74\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate (a) the gravitational field strength at its surface, (b) the gravitational force on a $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ person standing there and (c) the minimum speed with which a rocket must leave the surface to escape from the Moon. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}=\dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times7.35\times10^{22}}{(1.74\times10^{6})^2}=\mathbf{1.62\ N\,kg^{-1}}$.

(b) $F=mg=60\times1.62=\mathbf{97\ N}$, about $0.17$ of the person's weight on Earth.

(c) $v_e=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times7.35\times10^{22}}{1.74\times10^{6}}}=\mathbf{2370\ m\,s^{-1}}$.

items.enonce_markdown: A navigation satellite orbits the Earth in a circle with a period of $12$ hours. Use $GM=3.98\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-1}}$ for the Earth and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$. (a) Show that the radius of its orbit is $2.66\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$ and find its height above the surface. (b) Calculate its orbital speed. (c) Compare the radius with that of a geostationary orbit ($4.22\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$) using the relation between $T$ and $r$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $T=12\times3600=43\,200\ \mathrm{s}$. From $T^2=\dfrac{4\pi^2r^3}{GM}$,
$$r=\left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}=\left(\frac{3.98\times10^{14}\times(43\,200)^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}=\mathbf{2.66\times10^{7}\ m}$$
The height is $r-R_E=2.02\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

(b) $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi\times2.66\times10^{7}}{43\,200}=\mathbf{3870\ m\,s^{-1}}$.

(c) Since $T^2\propto r^3$, $r\propto T^{2/3}$. The period is half that of a geostationary satellite, so the radius is smaller by the factor $(1/2)^{2/3}=0.63$: $4.22\times10^{7}\times0.63=2.66\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$, which agrees with part (a).

items_markdown: Newton's law $F=GMm/r^2$ and the field $g=GM/r^2$ use $r$ measured between centres; the field is directed towards the mass and is inverse-square outside a sphere.
Inside a uniform sphere $g$ is proportional to the distance from the centre, so the graph of $g$ against $r$ rises to a maximum at the surface and then falls as $1/r^2$.
Gravitational potential $\phi=-GM/r$ is negative, $g=-\mathrm{d}\phi/\mathrm{d}r$, and escape speed follows from $\tfrac12mv_e^2=GMm/R$.
For a circular orbit gravity gives the centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$: $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/GM$.

Astronauts feel weightless because they are in free fall with the spacecraft, not because gravity vanishes; a geostationary satellite has a 24 hour period, orbits above the equator and moves from west to east.
